claim: A gain byte over a peaking section does not build the section at the gain it names. One section is stored at the top of the printed range and the byte blends it against the dry path, and a cut is that same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. The two readings agree at both ends of the window and at its centre and nowhere between, which is why nothing in this archive had noticed: at six decibels of a twelve decibel range the peak is about forty per cent narrower than the width byte asked for, and it is the width and not the height that says so -- every candidate here stands where the byte asked.
whyNotNamed: Whether the stored section is blended on the fly or a row per setting is held in ROM is not readable from outside the part: both give this curve at every setting. What is claimed is the curve and the two things about the part that produce it -- one stored section per entry rather than one per gain, and a cut that costs no second section.
adds: The records say what each setting of a gain byte did to the band profile. This claim is the step from that to how the byte reaches the section, which no record says and which the profile carries only in its width at the settings between the window's ends and its centre. What it adds over every model in this archive is that those models were wrong there: each of them builds its sections at the gain, and each of them was scored on records whose residual is smallest exactly where that is wrong.
refutedBy: A peaking section at half its gain coming back the width its width byte asks for. Or a cut coming back a different width from the boost of the same height. Or a setting in the middle of the window whose profile is not the blend's, at more than the one band this reading resolves.
whatItWouldChange: Every renderer of this line builds its equaliser sections at the gain asked for, because that is what a filter cookbook says to do. At the ends of the byte that is right and at every other setting it makes the peak too wide -- forty per cent at half gain, which is most of an octave on a mid section and is the part of a parametric equaliser a listener is setting the width byte for. It is also two lines of arithmetic to fix and it makes the gain cheaper rather than dearer.

eraPriors.claim: Building a filter section at an arbitrary gain is the expensive answer, and blending one stored section against the dry path is the cheap one.
eraPriors.why: The coefficients of a peaking section want a sine and a square root of the gain, which a small control processor would rather not run on every parameter change; storing them instead costs a row per setting of the gain, on top of a row per entry of the tables beside it. Blending is neither: mixing a section's transfer towards unity leaves its denominator alone and makes its numerator three multiply-accumulates between two stored rows.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The section at half its full gain had the width its width byte asks for, at a resolution the run can tell apart.

eraPriors.claim: A cut costs no second stored section.
eraPriors.why: The peaking section every filter cookbook of the period prints turns a boost into a cut by exchanging its numerator and its denominator, so a part that has the boost has the cut for nothing. A part that stored a second section at full cut and blended towards it instead would cut wider than it boosts, which is the asymmetry a constant-width graphic equaliser is known for.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: A cut of the same height as a boost came back a different width, which is what the second reading in this class predicts and what the cut side of these records was read for.

eraPriors.claim: What is worth saving a stored row on is a section with tables behind it, not a shelf with two states.
eraPriors.why: A mid section has sixteen centres and five widths behind it, so a row per gain setting would be eighty rows multiplied again. A shelf on this type has two corner states and no width, so there are two rows and nothing a blend would save.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The shelves turned out to be blended too, which the one record that sweeps a shelf gain finely was read for.

alternatives.reading: The section is the cookbook section computed at the gain the byte names, or read out of a row stored per setting, which is the same curve.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It says the feature is the width its width byte asked for at every setting of the gain, and the unit's is not: over 24 settings on two records it is out by 8.83 bands of a twelfth on average, always in the same direction, against the one band this reading resolves. Its residual over those records is three to five times the winner's.

alternatives.reading: The same blend, with the cut side blending towards a second section stored at full cut rather than inverting the boost.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It is the winner on the boost side and cannot be told from it there. On the cut side it makes the feature wider as the cut shallows where the unit makes it narrower: 15 settings wrong and 11.42 bands out on average. It is also the only candidate here whose residual leans on a record. A cut that is the boost's mirror is what a coefficient swap gives and what this unit does.

alternatives.reading: The same blend with the one stored section at the bottom of the printed range rather than the top, so the near side of the byte is the cut and the boost is that inverted.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It is this claim's winner turned over, it costs the same three multiply-accumulates, and it is the last of the four here: it makes the feature wider than the width byte asked for by about as much as building at the gain makes it wrong the other way -- 24 settings wrong and 16.45 bands out on average, the worst residual of the four, and the only reading here whose residual leans on two records. It is in the class because the shelves of this same type were measured to do it, which is why it was written and why the mid sections were put to it again.

alternatives.reading: The shelves are reached the same way, and what the shelf record shows is something about reading a shelf rather than about the path.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Half of it was right and the half that decides was not. The count this class uses on a peak is the wrong instrument on a shelf -- it counts up from the bottom of the band set -- so what that count showed was indeed about the reading. Read a shelf's own way, on the same record and the same takes, the shelves are blended and they are not reached the same way: the stored section is at the other end of the range, which is the winner here turned over and the last of the four on these records. inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-shelf-stores-the-cut.json.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  01 00  ·  section-gain
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/section-mixed-with-the-dry-path.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-stored-section-blended-with-the-dry.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
//
// Compared against the unit over:
//   40 03 09: Three settings, all of them the window's ends or its centre, so this address separates nothing here and is scored for the ends
//   40 03 0C: Settings [55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73] on three records, which are four to nine steps from the centre of the window on both sides
//   stimulus: A held note through the effect, its takes read as the energy of each twelfth octave against the run's own flat repeats.
//
// Outside that domain this says nothing: The two shelves of this type, which are read a
// shelf's own way and answer differently. Every other type that prints a gain against a
// peaking section -- six of them, none read for this. Settings one to three steps from the
// centre of the window, where the feature is too small for the band set to hold a width at
// all. What the part stores rather than computes, which no reading of an output reaches.
//
// Residual: 0.0039 median, 0.0063 worst, in the median residual in decibels over the span the byte commands, meaned over the records that carry a feature.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_00 {

// The unit's own output ends between sixteen and eighteen kilohertz, measured: thirty-two
// decibels over silence at sixteen, sixteen at seventeen, nothing at eighteen. A chain
// running at thirty-two kilohertz ends exactly there. The rate is part of the candidate
// rather than a constant, so a reading above the half-rate is dropped by name instead of
// being answered with a number the model never said.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A first-order shelf: one pole, one zero, tilting the two sides of its corner
 * against each other. `(s + w0 * V) / (s + w0)` for a low shelf and
 * `(V * s + w0) / (s + w0)` for a high one, bilinear-transformed.
 */
struct Shelf1 {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double v = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 20.0);
    const double k = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    const double norm = 1.0 / (1.0 + k);
    a1 = (k - 1.0) * norm;
    if (side == Side::Low) {
      b0 = (1.0 + v * k) * norm;
      b1 = (v * k - 1.0) * norm;
    } else {
      b0 = (v + k) * norm;
      b1 = (k - v) * norm;
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 - a1 * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

/** A second-order section, set the way the audio cookbook sets one. */
struct Biquad {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, b2 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, a2 = 0.0;
  double x1 = 0.0, x2 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0, y2 = 0.0;

  void setShelf(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double a = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 40.0);
    const double w = 2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz;
    const double cs = std::cos(w);
    // Unit slope, which is what `order 2` means here.
    const double alpha = std::sin(w) / 2.0 * std::sqrt(2.0);
    const double two = 2.0 * std::sqrt(a) * alpha;
    const double sign = side == Side::Low ? 1.0 : -1.0;
    const double a0 = (a + 1.0) - sign * (a - 1.0) * cs + two;
    b0 = a * ((a + 1.0) + sign * (a - 1.0) * cs + two) / a0;
    b1 = sign * 2.0 * a * ((a - 1.0) + sign * (a + 1.0) * cs) / a0;
    b2 = a * ((a + 1.0) + sign * (a - 1.0) * cs - two) / a0;
    a1 = -sign * 2.0 * ((a - 1.0) - sign * (a + 1.0) * cs) / a0;
    a2 = ((a + 1.0) - sign * (a - 1.0) * cs - two) / a0;
  }

  void setPeaking(double hz, double gainDb, double q) {
    const double a = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 40.0);
    const double w = 2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz;
    const double alpha = std::sin(w) / (2.0 * q);
    const double a0 = 1.0 + alpha / a;
    b0 = (1.0 + alpha * a) / a0;
    b1 = -2.0 * std::cos(w) / a0;
    b2 = (1.0 - alpha * a) / a0;
    a1 = b1;
    a2 = (1.0 - alpha / a) / a0;
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 + b2 * x2 - a1 * y1 - a2 * y2;
    x2 = x1;
    x1 = x;
    y2 = y1;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

}

/** The chain the model names, in the order it names it. */
struct Effect {
  Shelf1 shelf0;
  Biquad peaking1;
  Biquad peaking2;
  Shelf1 shelf3;
  double gain4 = 1.0;

  void prepare(int b40_03_03, int b40_03_04, int b40_03_07, int b40_03_09, int b40_03_08, int b40_03_0A, int b40_03_0C, int b40_03_0B, int b40_03_05, int b40_03_06, int b40_03_16) {
    shelf0.set(shelf0CornerHz(b40_03_03), shelf0GainDb(b40_03_04), Shelf1::Side::Low);
    peaking1.setPeaking(peaking1CentreHz(b40_03_07), peaking1GainDb(b40_03_09), peaking1Q(b40_03_08));
    peaking2.setPeaking(peaking2CentreHz(b40_03_0A), peaking2GainDb(b40_03_0C), peaking2Q(b40_03_0B));
    shelf3.set(shelf3CornerHz(b40_03_05), shelf3GainDb(b40_03_06), Shelf1::Side::High);
    gain4 = std::pow(10.0, (gain4GainDb(b40_03_16)) / 20.0);
  }

  double process(double x) {
    x = shelf0.process(x);
    x = peaking1.process(x);
    x = peaking2.process(x);
    x = shelf3.process(x);
    x *= gain4;
    return x;
  }
};

extra.key: a note on how it was nearly missed
extra.text: Three gates passed on the reading this refutes, on the same records, for two rounds. The residual is meaned over a record and the settings where the two readings differ are the ones whose profile is smallest, so they carry the least of the record's span; and the lean test looks for a residual that runs with the setting or with frequency, while this one is a hump -- nothing at both ends of the window and nothing at its centre. What found it was asking what the width was doing at the settings nobody had asked about, which is a reading and not a run.
